To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the risk per bronch cell of developing bronchial carcinoma increases with age, and with dose of cigarette smoke, and that the dependence on dose is not linear.

the annual lung cancer risk in the age range of 40-79 is 0.273X(10)(-12) times the number of cigarettes smoked daily to the power 2.5, multiplied by the number of years smoked to the power 4.5, multiplied for males by the number of pack years smoked to the 1.2 power, and for females by 0.8 times the number of pack-years.

(1) the lung cancer risk of regular cigarette smokers is strongly dependent on dose, with a highly significant (P less that 0.01), though probably non-linear, dose-response relationship in a range that includes the average dose for regular smokers; (2) the lung cancer risks of lifelong non-smokers are very small; (3) the lung cancer incidence of regular smokers is strongly dependent also on duration of smoking, and this dependence is approximately exponential, with a half-life for lung cancer
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions:1.
the relationship of dose and time to the incidence of lung cancer in cigarette smokers and lifelong non- smokers.
the dose-response relationship between smoking and lung cancer, and with the time-response relationship, in the sense of the age of onset of the disease in relation to the age of starting smoking.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

cigarette smoking is a necessary cause of bronchial cancer, that the risk per smoker increases with dose, that the risk of lung cancer per bronchial epithelial cell increases with the dose received by the cell, and that the dose received by a bronchial epithelium cell increases with the number of cigarettes smoked per day by the smoker.
cigarette smoking is a major risk factor for bronchial carcinoma, and that there is some evidence that the relationship between risk and dose is not exactly linear.

cigarette smoking is causally related to bronchial carcinoma and that the dose-response relationship between cigarette smoking and bronchal carcinoma is not linear, but that there is no evidence of any threshold for this effect.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the dose-response relationship for lung cancer incidence among cigarette smokers is not only statistically significant but is also of such a magnitude that the risk of lung cancer among cigarette smokers is very much greater than that among non-smokers.
the dose-response curve is not a straight line but that there is no evidence of a threshold dose.
the dose-response relationship between cigarette smoking and bronchogenic carcinoma is probably curvilinear and that this may help explain the anatomical distribution of the disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the risk of lung cancer is strongly related to smoking, and this relationship is not linear.
smoking is a major cause of lung cancer, and that the more you smoke, the more likely you are to get lung cancer.
the risk of lung cancer from smoking is not just a simple linear relationship with the number of cigarettes smoked.
